commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename Duke to Erina, add greeting and farewell
commitResults.messageBody:
The template ships with a placeholder class named Duke. Rename it to
  Erina, the name chosen for this chatbot, so the class, file, banner art
  and user-facing docs all agree. The rename was made with git mv so the
  file's history is preserved rather than recorded as a delete plus an add.

  Erina now greets the user on startup and prints a farewell before
  terminating, completing the three parts of Level-0 (rename, greet, exit).
  Replies are wrapped in horizontal rules; this is the format the later
  increments expect once the program starts reading user input.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-1: Echo user input until bye
commitResults.messageBody:
Erina now reads commands from standard input and repeats each one back,
  ending the conversation when the user types bye.

  Reading uses Scanner.hasNextLine() so that input ending without an
  explicit bye exits cleanly instead of throwing NoSuchElementException.

  The divider-wrapped output shared by the greeting, the farewell and the
  echo is pulled into a single reply() helper, so the reply format is
  defined in one place as later increments add more kinds of output.

Text that is not a recognised command is now stored as a task and
confirmed with 'added: <task>', and the list command prints every stored
task numbered from 1.

Tasks are held in an ArrayList rather than the fixed 100-element array
suggested by the exercise, so there is no arbitrary capacity and no
separate counter to keep in step with the contents.

The list is passed to addTask and listTasks as a parameter rather than
kept in a static field, so each method states what it operates on; this
is also a smaller step towards the TaskList object of later increments.

Listing an empty list shows a prompt rather than an empty divider block,
which otherwise looked like the command had failed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Mark tasks as done or not done
commitResults.messageBody:
A task is now a description plus a completion flag, so it is modelled as
a Task object rather than a bare String. Holding both fields in one
object means they cannot fall out of step, and gives later increments a
place to add per-task behaviour.

The mark and unmark commands take a task number, so input is now split
into a command word and its argument instead of being matched whole. The
displayed number counts from 1 and is converted to a 0-based index at the
point of use.

The list command now shows a heading and each task's status box.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-4: Add to-do, deadline and event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks now come in three kinds, each shown with its own type box: [T] for
a plain to-do, [D] for a task due by a stated time, and [E] for one
spanning a period.

Task becomes abstract with Todo, Deadline and Event extending it. The
description and completion flag stay in the parent so they are written
once, while each subclass overrides toString to prepend its type box and
append any extra detail. Making Task abstract states that every task the
user can create is one of these three kinds.

Deadline and Event keep their times as the text the user typed; a later
increment replaces these with a real date type.

Adding a task now reports the new task count, and unrecognised input gets
a message instead of being stored as a task. Level-5 replaces that ad-hoc
message with proper exception handling.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Explain errors instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Erina now rejects commands it cannot carry out with a message the user
can act on, rather than throwing a stack trace or silently doing the
wrong thing. Unknown commands, missing descriptions, missing /by, /from
and /to parts, non-numeric task numbers and out-of-range task numbers are
all covered.

Failures are carried by a new ErinaException. It extends Exception rather
than RuntimeException so the compiler forces callers to deal with it,
which is exactly the intent: these errors exist to be reported to the
user. Its message is written in plain language because it is shown as-is.

The main loop catches ErinaException in one place, so a failed command
never ends the conversation and there is a single definition of what a
rejected command looks like. NumberFormatException from parsing a task
number is rethrown as an ErinaException so the loop handles one kind of
failure.

Task-number validation is centralised in parseIndex, so every command
taking a number checks it the same way. The command chain becomes a
switch now that there are six commands, and blank input lines are
skipped rather than reported as errors.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-6: Delete tasks from the list
commitResults.messageBody:
The delete command removes a task and reports what was removed together
with the new task count. List.remove returns the task it took out, so
the removed task can still be shown to the user after it has left the
list.

Task-number validation reuses parseIndex, so delete rejects missing,
non-numeric and out-of-range numbers with the same wording as mark and
unmark, and remaining tasks renumber automatically because positions are
derived from the list rather than stored.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: Represent commands as an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
The seven String command constants and the switch over raw strings are
replaced by a Command enum, so the instructions Erina accepts are stated
in one enumerable place rather than scattered as quoted literals that the
compiler cannot check.

Command.fromKeyword is now the single point at which typed text becomes a
known command, so it is also the single place that can decide the text is
not one; the unknown-command error moves there from the switch default.

Switching over the enum lets the compiler check cases against the
declared set, which a switch over String cannot do. BYE joins the same
mechanism instead of being special-cased ahead of the try block, though
the main loop still handles it since only the loop can stop reading.

Task types deliberately stay as subclasses rather than becoming an enum:
the type box and extra detail are already handled by each subclass's
toString, and an enum there would duplicate that.

Behaviour is unchanged; the full command and error regression produces
identical output to Level-6.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Save tasks to the hard disk
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list is now written to data/erina.txt after every change and
loaded back when the program starts, so tasks survive between runs.

Each task is one line in the file, produced by a new toSaveString method
on Task. Each kind of task decides its own save form the same way it
decides its own toString; the two stay separate methods because the save
form is machine-facing and must stay stable while toString is user-facing
and free to change.

A new Storage class owns all reading and writing of the file. Saving
happens in one place in the main loop, after every successful command,
so the file always matches the list and no command has to remember to
save. Loading treats a missing file as a normal first run; a file that
cannot be understood is reported with its line number and the program
starts with an empty list rather than dying, keeping the unreadable file
on disk until the user changes something.

The data folder is gitignored because the save file is user data, not
source.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Store deadline dates as real dates
commitResults.messageBody:
The /by part of a deadline is now parsed as a LocalDate, entered as
yyyy-mm-dd and shown as MMM d yyyy, so 2019-10-15 is displayed as
Oct 15 2019.

Keeping a real date rather than the text the user typed means the date
can be reformatted for display now, and compared and sorted in later
increments. Text that is not a date in that form is rejected with a
message showing the expected format, including impossible dates such as
2019-13-40, which LocalDate.parse refuses.

The save file keeps the ISO yyyy-mm-dd form, which LocalDate prints and
parses natively, so the file stays readable and round-trips without a
custom format. A saved date that cannot be parsed is treated like any
other corrupted line: reported with its line number, after which the
program starts with an empty list.

Events keep their from and to parts as text for now: the course sets
deadlines as the minimum for this increment, and events would also need
times of day rather than bare dates to be worth converting.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Extract Ui, Parser and TaskList classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Erina had grown into one class that talked to the user, parsed input,
held the tasks and coordinated saving. Those are four different reasons
to change, so each moves to its own class:

Ui owns all reading and printing, so the rest of the program deals in
what to say while one class decides how it looks; a later GUI touches
only this class. Parser owns all knowledge of command syntax (/by and
/from markers, date format, task numbering), so the rest of the program
never inspects raw text. TaskList wraps the list of tasks and gives
list-wide behaviour added later, such as searching, one natural home.
Storage was already extracted in Level-7.

Erina keeps only coordination: it wires the parts together and maps each
command to the right calls. It is now an object rather than a bag of
static methods, so main simply creates one and runs it.

Pure refactoring: a scripted session covering every command and error
path produces byte-identical output and an identical save file before
and after.

All classes move out of the default package: the coordinator and
infrastructure classes into erina, and the Task hierarchy into
erina.task. The task classes form a natural unit that the rest of the
code uses only through Task and the parsers, which is what the package
boundary now states.

The default package also cannot be imported from named packages, so
moving out of it is a prerequisite for JUnit test classes, which live in
their own source tree and import the classes under test.

Files were moved with git mv so their history is preserved. The README's
setup instructions now point at the file's new location. Pure
refactoring: the scripted session again produces byte-identical output
and an identical save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Gradle: Adapt the Gradle build to this project
commitResults.messageBody:
The course-provided add-gradle-support branch is merged in, bringing
Gradle 9.6.1 with the application, shadow and JUnit setup already
configured for Java 25.

Two settings are adapted from the Duke template this project no longer
matches: the application main class becomes erina.Erina, and the fat jar
produced by shadowJar is named erina.jar.

Verified with ./gradlew build and by running the app through ./gradlew
run.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JUnit: Add JUnit tests for Parser, TaskList and Deadline
commitResults.messageBody:
Sixteen tests across three classes, run through Gradle's test task.

Parser gets the most attention because it is where user input can go
wrong: each parse method is covered for its normal case and its error
cases (empty description, missing /by, text instead of a date,
impossible dates, non-numeric and out-of-range task numbers), asserting
on the user-facing message where its exact wording matters.

TaskList is covered for growth, ordering, and that removing a task
returns it and closes the gap. DeadlineTest pins down the two date
forms, readable for display and ISO for saving, which must not drift
apart since the save form has to round-trip through LocalDate.parse.

Test names follow the unitBeingTested_descriptionOfTestInputs_
expectedOutcome convention from the course testing guidance.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JavaDoc: Complete Javadoc for all public API
commitResults.messageBody:
Classes and non-trivial methods were documented as they were written,
so this increment closes the remaining gaps the javadoc tool warned
about: @return tags on the single-line-documented getters, a comment on
main, and an explicit documented constructor for Ui in place of the
undocumented default one.

The javadoc task now runs with zero warnings, which also gives a simple
regression check for future changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Import Pattern instead of qualifying it inline
commitResults.messageBody:
The one deviation a sweep against the course Java coding standard found:
Storage referred to java.util.regex.Pattern by its fully qualified name
inside an expression, where the standard expects an import. The sweep
also confirmed line length, indentation, brace style, naming and import
ordering are already compliant, and the Git side (imperative commit
subjects, branch and tag naming) follows the course conventions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Find tasks by searching descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
The find command shows the tasks whose descriptions contain the given
text, numbered from 1 by their position among the matches, matching the
course sample output. Matches ignore case, since a user searching is
after the task, not the capitalisation they typed it with; searching for
nothing is rejected, and a search with no matches says so rather than
printing an empty block.

The search itself lives in TaskList.find, the kind of list-wide
behaviour that class was extracted to hold, and comes with tests for
case-insensitive matching, order preservation and the no-match case.
Erina only formats the result.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CheckStyle: Enforce the coding standard automatically
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds the Gradle checkstyle plugin with the course configuration, so the
Java coding standard is checked by the build rather than by eye. A
CodingStandard sweep last week was manual; this makes it a build step
that cannot be forgotten.

The tool found 52 violations that reading had missed, all now fixed:

- 37 Indentation: case labels sat level with their switch instead of
  being indented inside it.
- 14 CustomImportOrder: the project's own erina.* imports came before
  java.*; the standard wants static, then java, then org, then com, then
  everything else, each group separated and alphabetical.
- 1 DeclarationOrder: the Ui constructor added during A-JavaDoc was
  declared above the field it initialises.

checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest now pass with zero violations, and the
build, tests and a scripted session confirm behaviour is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011LddqwD1Y4PsnnaP61Eb7W

Erina now opens a window with a scrolling conversation, a text field and a
Send button, following the structure of the course JavaFX tutorial:
Launcher starts the app to avoid the module path issue, Main loads
MainWindow.fxml, and DialogBox pairs each message with a picture, flipped
so the user and Erina are easy to tell apart.

The build.gradle JavaFX dependency block is taken from the tutorial as
given, including all three OS classifiers so the project builds
everywhere. On this machine the runtime actually comes from the JavaFX
bundled in the mandated Azul JDK 25, which the startup log confirms by
loading javafx.graphics from jrt: rather than from a jar. That is also
why the tutorial's Intel-only mac classifier is not a problem here.

To let the GUI and the console share one implementation, command handling
now returns what Erina wants to say instead of printing it, in a new
getResponse method. The console loop prints the result, the GUI puts it
in a dialog box, and behaviour cannot drift between them. Loading the
save file moves into the constructor so both front ends report a bad file
the same way.

The text UI is kept, which the exercise allows: it costs one thin method,
keeps the existing tests meaningful, and makes the core easy to exercise
without driving a window. A scripted session confirms console output is
byte-identical to before this change.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Varargs: Build multi-line replies with a varargs helper
commitResults.messageBody:
Erina built its multi-line replies with four separate String.join calls.
They now go through a respond(String... lines) helper, so a reply reads
as its lines, one per argument, in the same shape as the Ui.reply method
that has taken varargs since Level-1. Callers that already hold an array
of lines pass it straight in, which is the other half of what varargs
gives you.

This is the smallest change that applies varargs deliberately rather than
incidentally; the alternative was to tag the existing Ui.reply usage with
no code change at all.

A scripted session confirms console output is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011LddqwD1Y4PsnnaP61Eb7W

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Assertions: Document internal assumptions with assert
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods rely on conditions that earlier code has already
guaranteed, but nothing states those conditions where they are relied
upon. A reader of TaskList.get, for example, cannot tell that the index
has already been validated by Parser.parseIndex, and a future change
that breaks that guarantee would fail somewhere far from its cause.

Java's assert statement is the right tool here: it documents the
assumption at the point of use, and checks it during development
without adding runtime checks (or user-facing error handling) for
situations that are bugs rather than user errors.

Let's,
* assert the pre-conditions of TaskList (index in range, non-null task)
  and the post-condition of Parser.parseIndex (a 0-based index in range)
* assert that constructors of Task, Deadline and Event receive the
  fields they need, since Parser and Storage validate those first
* assert in Erina that bye never reaches handleCommand, that
  Command.fromKeyword never returns null, and that adding a task grows
  the list by exactly one
* assert in Storage that parseTask always yields a task, and in
  DialogBox that the FXML injected both controls
* enable assertions for the Gradle run task, since the JVM disables
  them by default

Assertions are deliberately not used for user input or save-file
contents: those are external and keep their ErinaException handling.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract the numbered task listing shared by list and find
commitResults.messageBody:
The list and find commands each build a heading followed by one
numbered line per task, using the same loop and the same "n." format.
The two copies have already started to drift: only one explains why
the display number is i + 1, and a change to the layout (say, aligning
the numbers) would have to be made twice and could easily be made once.

Let's move that loop into a numberedList(heading, tasks) helper that
both commands call. Each command now reads at one level of abstraction:
decide what to show, then hand the tasks over to be formatted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: Assemble a task's save line and display form in Task itself
commitResults.messageBody:
Todo, Deadline and Event each build their own save line, so the layout
of that line (type letter, then a 1/0 done flag, then the description,
all separated by " | ") is repeated three times, and the separator is
spelled out a fourth time in Storage, which has to split on it. The
same three classes also repeat the "[T]" style type tag in toString().
Adding a kind of task, or changing the format, means editing every one
of those places in step.

Let's have Task assemble both forms. A subclass now only states its
type code and, if it has any, the extra fields it needs saved:
* getTypeCode() supplies the letter used by both the save line and the
  display tag, so the two can no longer disagree
* getExtraSaveFields() returns the fields after the description; the
  default is none, which is what a plain to-do needs
* SAVE_SEPARATOR is defined once, in Task, and Storage splits on it

Todo loses its overrides entirely, and Deadline and Event keep only the
detail that is genuinely theirs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: Move command-word parsing from Erina into Parser
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser's contract is that all knowledge of the command syntax lives in
it and the rest of the program never inspects raw input. Erina.getResponse
breaks that: it trims the line, splits off the first word and decides
what counts as the argument, before Parser gets involved at all. That
leaves getResponse working at two levels at once (string surgery, then
dispatching commands), and puts part of the syntax where nobody would
look for it.

Let's add Parser.parse(input), which returns the command and its
argument together as a ParsedCommand record. getResponse now reads as
"parse, then dispatch", and a change to how a line is split (say,
allowing tabs) is again a change to Parser alone. The new method gets
its own unit tests alongside the other Parser tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the default save file location in one place
commitResults.messageBody:
Both the console entry point (Erina) and the GUI entry point (Main)
declare their own SAVE_FILE constant with the same "data/erina.txt"
value. Nothing ties the two together, so moving the save file would be
a two-place change, and the two front ends could silently end up
reading different files.

Let's make Erina the single owner of that decision: it exposes
DEFAULT_SAVE_FILE and gains a no-argument constructor that uses it.
Main just asks for a default Erina. The constructor that takes a path
stays, since tests and future features (a user-chosen data file) still
need it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove repeated messages and inconsistent reply building
commitResults.messageBody:
Three small readability problems, all of the "say it once" kind:

* Parser.parseEvent spells out the same long error message twice, so
  the two copies can drift apart. Let's name it once as a constant.
* Erina.handleCommand's default branch repeats the "I don't know what
  that means" message that Command.fromKeyword already owns. But that
  branch can only be reached by a programming error (an enum value
  that nobody handles), never by a user, so a user-facing message is
  the wrong response. Let's throw IllegalStateException instead, which
  is both honest about what happened and drops the duplicate text.
* setDone builds its reply with an inline "\n", while every other
  command uses the respond(...) helper that exists for exactly this.
  Let's use respond there too, so all replies are built the same way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011PGkP5HtFok6kvTgftxwX8

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Streams: Replace collection loops with streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Four places walk a collection by hand to filter, transform or number
its elements: TaskList.find collects matches, Storage.save turns tasks
into lines, Command.fromKeyword searches the enum values, and Erina
numbers the tasks it lists. Each loop mixes the bookkeeping (an index,
a result list, an early return) with the one line that actually says
what is wanted.

Streams let each of those read as a description of the result instead:
* find becomes filter + toList
* save becomes map(Task::toSaveString) + toList
* fromKeyword becomes filter + findFirst, with the not-found case made
  explicit through Optional rather than by falling off the end of a loop
* the numbered listing becomes an IntStream over the positions, which
  gives the number and the task together

The checked ErinaException in fromKeyword is thrown outside the stream
pipeline, since lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions.

A-Streams: Replace collection loops with streams

commitResults.messageTitle: C-Help: Add a help command that lists every command
commitResults.messageBody:
A new user has no way to discover what Erina understands: the greeting
just asks "What can I do for you?", and a wrong guess gets "I don't
know what that means" with no hint about what would be right. The only
documentation is outside the app.

Let's add in-app guidance:
* a help command that lists every command with how to type it and what
  it does, plus a note on the date format
* the greeting now says to type help
* the unknown-command message now points to help as well

The help text is generated from the Command enum, which now carries a
usage line and a short description for each command. That keeps the
list of commands and the help text in one place, so a command added
later shows up in help automatically and the two cannot drift apart.
